where D0 is a set of negative and D1 positive examples ("Calders & Jaroszewicz, 2007).
It summarizes the curve into one number, measuring the model’s ability to distinguish
27

[Halaman 28]
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
between classes across all thresholds. It is threshold-independent and provides a balanced
performance view, especially in class imbalance cases with an expected value of 0.5 for
each random ranking (Hamer et al., 2023).
In addition to individually reporting the results for both training scenarios, we compute the aggregate
performance score averaged across the complete benchmark. We aim to facilitate a quick and
comprehensive comparison between models.
C.6 V ALIDATION
Due to the extensive empirical experiments and the volume of the training datasets required to produce
our baseline results for our benchmark within the BirdSet collection, traditional hyperparameter
optimization was not feasible. Additionally, the covariate shift between focals in training and
soundscapes in testing complicates result validation. Utilizing a validation split from the training
data is only partially functional, as it does not accurately represent the soundscape data distribution.
Furthermore, obtaining soundscapes from the test dataset for validation could introduce test data
leakage due to the static nature of soundscape recordings. Therefore, we follow (Hamer et al., 2023)
and employ the soundscape dataset POW for validation. However, this approach only allows us to
validate the results of the MT and LT training scenarios since DT has dedicated classes that are not
available in the validation dataset. In this case, we used a validation split from the training data and
employed augmentations.

We used the validation dataset to select the best-performing model based on the lowest loss across all
training epochs on POW. We show exemplary results of the validation loss curves for the training
scenario LT in Figure 10. It illustrates that more complex models with extensive parameters (AST
and ConvNext) tend to overfit early on the focal training data. In contrast, the smaller model (EAT)
benefits from extended training duration. More detailed results are available on Weights&Biases.

E D ATASHEET
This section provides a comprehensive and structured datasheet BirdSet, following the guidelines
outlined by Gebru et al. (2021). We aim to enhance clarity and facilitate effective communication
between us and researchers who wish to utilize the dataset collection. The datasheet comprises the
dataset’s motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing steps, uses, distribution, and
maintenance.
E.1 M OTIVATION
For what purpose was the dataset created? Was there a specific task in mind? Was there a specific
gap that needed to be filled? Please provide a description.
The BirdSet dataset collection was created to address the demand for a large-scale audio represen-
tation learning dataset, including a real-world evaluation test set. In addition, BirdSet serves as a
standardized dataset and evaluation protocol in computational avian bioacoustics. The specific task
is the classification of bird vocalizations in a realistic passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) scenario.
The goal was to consolidate fragmented research efforts, improve reproducibility, comparability, and
accessibility, and ultimately enhance the effectiveness of deep learning (DL) models in analyzing
bird vocalizations.
Who created the dataset (e.g., which team, research group) and on behalf of which entity (e.g.,
company, institution, organization)? If there is an associated grant, please provide the name of the
grantor and the grant name and number.
The dataset collection was created by a collaborative effort of researchers from the University of
Kassel at the Intelligent Embedded Systems group (IES), Kiel University at the Intelligent Systems
group (INS), Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Economics and Energy System Technology (IEE), and
TU Chemnitz. Throughout the creation of the dataset, the following people have been involved:
Lukas Rauch (IES), Raphael Schwinger (CAU), Moritz Wirth (IEE), and René Heinrich (IEE).
Who funded the creation of the dataset? The research was funded by the German Ministry for
Environment, Nature Conservation, Nuclear Safety, and Consumer Protection through the project
"DeepBirdDetect - Automatic Bird Detection of Endangered Species Using Deep Neural Networks"
(grant numbers: 67KI31040A, 67KI31040B, 67KI31040C).
Any other comments? A more detailed motivation and corresponding objectives can be found in the
main article.
E.2 C OMPOSITION
What do the instances that comprise the dataset represent (e.g., documents, photos, people,
countries)? Are there multiple types of instances (e.g., movies, users, and ratings; people and
interactions between them; nodes and edges)? Please provide a description.
The instances in the dataset collection are comprised of audio recordings of bird vocalizations in
their natural habitats. These include focal recordings from Xeno-Canto (XC), actively recorded by a
recordist for training purposes, and soundscape recordings captured by omnidirectional microphones
and annotated by experts for testing. For more detailed information on the unified metadata provided
for each instance, refer to Table 5.
How many instances are there in total (of each type, if appropriate)?
The dataset contains a total of 712,515 instances. It includes over 520,000 focal recordings from
various locations worldwide and over 400 hours of soundscape recordings from passive acoustic
monitoring (PAM) scenarios in South America, North America, and Europe. For more details, refer
to Figure 7, Figure 8, Figure 5, and the main article.
Does the dataset contain all possible instances, or is it a sample (not necessarily random) of
instances from a larger set? If the dataset is a sample, then what is the larger set? Is the
sample representative of the larger set (e.g., geographic coverage)? If so, please describe how
this representativeness was validated/verified. If it is not representative of the larger set, please
33

[Halaman 34]
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
describe why not (e.g., to cover a more diverse range of instances because instances were withheld
or unavailable)
The dataset is a curated collection of publicly available recordings, primarily sourced from the
platforms XC (Vellinga & Planqué, 2015) and Zenodo (CERN). We included all available recordings
from XC as of 03/10/2024 in the XCL dataset, excluding those with an ND license. Additionally, we
omitted recordings of highly endangered bird species. The XCM dataset, a subset of XCL, contains
all bird species present across the test dataset. We also provide dedicated training datasets containing
only the species represented in each test dataset. Selected test datasets from Zenodo are incorporated
as available. Further details can be found in the main article.
What data does each instance consist of? "Raw" data (e.g., unprocessed text or images) or features?
In either case, please provide a description
An instance consists of a raw audio recording with a resolution of 32 kHz in the .OGG format and
respective metadata detailed in Table 5. We also provide a list of possible vocalization events for each
training recording.
Is there a label or target associated with each instance? If so, please provide a description.
Each instance is labeled with the eBird taxonomy (Sullivan et al., 2009) from 2021 corresponding to
the bird species in the recording.
Is any information missing from individual instances? If so, please provide a description, ex-
plaining why this information is missing (e.g., because it was unavailable). This does not include
intentionally removed information but might include, e.g., redacted text.
No information from the source datasets has been removed. However, some recordings in the
training datasets have incomplete metadata and annotations. While secondary bird vocalizations are
sometimes annotated, they are not always identified. Additionally, it may not always be clear which
events belong to the primary bird species or secondary background species. More information on
label uncertainty is provided in the main article.
Are relationships between individual instances made explicit (e.g., users’ movie ratings, social
network links)? If so, please describe how these relationships are made explicit.
Relationships between instances are not explicitly defined, as each recording is treated independently
for the classification tasks. However, the metadata includes details such as the recordist, location,
and recording device, allowing for identifying similar instances. The soundscape test datasets are
recorded in static environments where segments have inherent relationships that are valuable for
real-world applications. These relationships are not considered in our benchmark.
Are there recommended data splits (e.g., training, development/validation, testing)? If so, please
provide a description of these splits, explaining the rationale behind them.
The dataset collection is split into training and testing datasets. Training datasets (XCL , XCM) are
used to train large-scale models, while soundscape recordings (e.g., PER, NES, UHH ) are used for
testing. This split reflects practical PAM scenarios, where models are trained on a broad dataset and
evaluated on realistic, strongly-labeled soundscapes. Additionally, we provide a validation dataset
(POW) for tuning hyperparameters or validating model results. Additionally, we provide small
fine-tuning training datasets for each test dataset with a randomly generated validation split during
training.
Are there any errors, sources of noise, or redundancies in the dataset? If so, please provide a
description.
Potential noise sources in the recordings include background sounds inherent to the natural envi-
ronments where the data were collected. These are not typical errors but reflect the real-world
conditions under which bird vocalizations occur. Additionally, the training recordings from XC are
weakly labeled, meaning the exact timing of the vocalization events within the recordings is uncertain.
Further details on label uncertainty are provided in the main paper.
Is the dataset self-contained, or does it link to or otherwise rely on external resources (e.g.,
websites, tweets, other datasets)? If it links to or relies on external resources, a) are there guarantees
that they will exist, and remain constant, over time; b) are there official archival versions of the
34

[Halaman 35]
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
complete dataset (i.e., including the external resources as they existed at the time the dataset was
created); c) are there any restrictions (e.g., licenses, fees) associated with any of the external resources
that might apply to a dataset consumer? Please provide descriptions of all external resources and
any restrictions associated with them, as well as links or other access points, as appropriate.
The dataset is self-contained, with an internal backup ensuring its permanence and consistency over
time. Given the dynamic nature of XC and the availability of additional data, the training datasets are
designed to be expandable. Moreover, the metadata for each instance includes links to the original
sources, facilitating easy access and verification.
Does the dataset contain data that might be considered confidential (e.g., data that is pro-
tected by legal privilege or by doctor-patient confidentiality, data that includes the content of
individuals’ non-public communications)? If so, please provide a description.
All metadata adheres to the licensing terms of the respective recordings on XC (including the
recordists’ names) and Zenodo.
Does the dataset contain data that, if viewed directly, might be offensive, insulting, threatening,
or might otherwise cause anxiety?
No, the dataset collection only contains audio recordings of bird vocalizations, which are not offensive
or threatening.
Does the dataset identify any subpopulations (e.g., by age, gender)If so, please describe how these
subpopulations are identified and provide a description of their respective distributions within the
dataset.
The dataset does not identify subpopulations based on demographic factors; it focuses solely on bird
species.
Is it possible to identify individuals (i.e., one or more natural persons), either directly or
indirectly (i.e., in combination with other data) from the dataset? If so, please describe how
The metadata includes the recordist’s name and the recording location, which may indirectly provide
information about the recordist. The respective licenses of the XC recordings also include these
details.
Does the dataset contain data that might be considered sensitive in any way (e.g., data that
reveals race or ethnic origins, sexual orientations, religious beliefs, political opinions or union
memberships, or locations; financial or health data; biometric or genetic data; forms of
government identification, such as social security numbers; criminal history)? If so, please
provide a description.
No, the dataset does not contain sensitive data.
Any other comments?
No further comments.
E.3 C OLLECTION PROCESS
How was the data associated with each instance acquired? Was the data directly observable (e.g.,
raw text, movie ratings), reported by subjects (e.g., survey responses), or indirectly inferred/derived
from other data (e.g., part-of-speech tags, model-based guesses for age or language)? If the data was
reported by subjects or indirectly inferred/derived from other data, was the data validated/verified?
If so, please describe how.
The data was downloaded from the XC and Zenodo platforms. Download and preprocessing scripts
are available in the GitHub repository.
What mechanisms or procedures were used to collect the data (e.g., hardware apparatuses or
sensors, manual human curation, software programs, software APIs)? How were these mechanisms
or procedures validated?
We collected the data via the XC API and Zenodo. The recordings were captured using equipment
suitable for recording bird vocalizations. The recordings were manually curated and annotated by
35

[Halaman 36]
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
experts or enthusiasts. For further details, see the descriptions of the individual datasets listed in
Section B.
If the dataset is a sample from a larger set, what was the sampling strategy (e.g., deterministic,
probabilistic with specific sampling probabilities)?
The dataset is a curated collection from larger collections, specifically from the open-source platforms
XC and Zenodo. We exclude all recordings from XC that are licensed as CC-ND and sample based
on our training scenarios; the snapshot date is 03/10/2024. The selected datasets from Zenodo are
utilized as provided. See section B and the main article for further information.
Who was involved in the data collection process (e.g., students, crowd workers, contractors) and
how were they compensated (e.g., how much were crowd workers paid)?
The data collection involved researchers from several institutions, including the University of Kassel,
Kiel University, Fraunhofer Institute, and TU Chemnitz. The researchers were compensated according
to their contracts. The annotators of the focal recordings freely uploaded their recordings and
annotations to XC under respective licenses.
Over what timeframe was the data collected? Does this timeframe match the creation timeframe
of the data associated with the instances (e.g., recent crawl of new news articles)? If not, please
describe the timeframe in which the data associated with the instances was created.
The recordings were collected over several years on XC, with the date of each recording included in
the metadata. A snapshot from XC was taken on 03/10/2024.
Did you collect the data from the individuals in question directly or obtain it via third parties
or other sources (e.g., websites)?
The data was obtained from third-party sources, primarily the open-source platforms XC for training
and Zenodo for testing datasets.
Were the individuals in question notified about the data collection? If so, please describe (or
show with screenshots or other information) how notice was provided, and provide a link or other
access point to, or otherwise reproduce, the exact language of the notification itself.
The dataset collection includes only recordings that are properly licensed for use. All recordings are
under a creative commons (CC) license, summarized by our collection with the license CC-BY-NC-
SA.
Did the individuals in question consent to the collection and use of their data? If so, please
describe (or show with screenshots or other information) how consent was requested and provided,
and provide a link or other access point to, or otherwise reproduce, the exact language to which the
individuals consented.
We included only recordings with a proper CC license that permits usage.
If consent was obtained, were the consenting individuals provided with a mechanism to revoke
their consent in the future or for certain uses? If so, please provide a description, as well as a link
or other access point to the mechanism (if appropriate).
See above.
Has an analysis of the potential impact of the dataset and its use on data subjects (e.g., a data
protection impact analysis) been conducted? If so, please provide a description of this analysis,
including the outcomes, as well as a link or other access point to any supporting documentation.
No formal analysis has been conducted. However, all the data has already been publicly available
before.
Any other comments?
No further comments.

E.4 P REPROCESSING /C LEANING /LABELING
Was any preprocessing/cleaning/labeling of the data done (e.g., discretization or bucketing,
tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, SIFT feature extraction, removal of instances, processing
of missing values)? If so, please provide a description. If not, you may skip the remaining questions
in this section.
The audio recordings have been converted to the .OGG format and standardized to a 32kHz resolution.
Metadata has been standardized, and scientific bird species names have been unified to eBird (Sullivan
et al., 2009) codes as labels. Refer to Table 5 for a comprehensive overview of the metadata.
Additionally, we identified potential bird vocalization events from XC using thebambird (Michaud
et al., 2023) event detection algorithm and scipy peak detection. The soundscape recordings have
also been processed and are provided in 5-second segments for evaluation. For more details, refer to
our Hugging Face Dataset collection.
Was the "raw" data saved in addition to the preprocessed/cleaned/labeled data (e.g., to support
unanticipated future uses)? If so, please provide a link or other access point to the "raw" data.
The raw recordings remain accessible at their original sources. We also maintain an internal server
backup of all data for added security and reliability.
Is the software that was used to preprocess/clean/label the data available? If so, please provide a
link or other access point.
Code used for processing is available at our GitHub repository. Additionally, we detail the utilized
software assets above.
Any other comments?
No further comments.
E.5 U SES
Has the dataset been used for any tasks already? If so, please provide a description.
Yes, the dataset has been used in multi-label experiments in a PAM scenario with different training
protocols outlined in the main paper. Additionally, the dataset has been used for other internal
experiments in the context of the research project "DeepBirdDetect".
Is there a repository that links to any or all papers or systems that use the dataset? If so, please
provide a link or other access point.
To date, no papers have utilized this dataset.
What (other) tasks could the dataset be used for?
The BirdSet dataset collection can be used for various tasks beyond multi-label classification,
including but not limited to:
• Audio representation learning,
• Audio event detection,
• Noisy label learning,
• Few-Shot Learning,
• Domain adaption under covariate shift,
• Active learning,
• Conducting conservation research by monitoring bird populations and behaviors.
Is there anything about the composition of the dataset or the way it was collected and pre-
processed/cleaned/labeled that might impact future uses? For example, is there anything that a
dataset consumer might need to know to avoid uses that could result in unfair treatment of individuals
or groups (e.g., stereotyping, quality of service issues) or other risks or harms (e.g., legal risks,
financial harms)? If so, please provide a description. Is there anything a dataset consumer could do
to mitigate these risks or harms?
37

[Halaman 38]
Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
The dataset is composed of audio recordings of bird vocalizations and related metadata. Since it does
not involve human subjects, there are no risks of unfair treatment of individuals or groups. However,
users should be aware of the inherent variability in recording conditions (e.g., background noise,
distance from the sound source) and the potential for label noise due to the challenges in accurately
annotating bird calls in natural environments.
Are there tasks for which the dataset should not be used? If so, please provide a description. The
dataset should not be used to train models that can identify critically endangered bird species.
Any other comments?
No further comments.
E.6 D ISTRIBUTION
Will the dataset be distributed to third parties outside of the entity (e.g., company, institution,
organization) on behalf of which the dataset was created? If so, please provide a description.
Yes, see the next question.
How will the dataset be distributed (e.g., tarball on website, API, GitHub)? Does the dataset
have a digital object identifier (DOI)?
The dataset is available on Hugging Face with a respective DOI. Additionally, the metadata, including
links to the sources, is available in our GitHub repository, allowing for dataset construction without
using Hugging Face.
When will the dataset be distributed?
It is already public.
Will the dataset be distributed under a copyright or other intellectual property (IP) license,
and/or under applicable terms of use (ToU)? If so, please describe this license and/or ToU, and
provide a link or other access point to, or otherwise reproduce, any relevant licensing terms or ToU,

The effect of soundscape composition on bird vocalization classification in

ARTICLE INFO

ABSTRACT
There is a need for monitoring biodiversity at multiple spatial and temporal scales to aid conservation efforts.
Autonomous recording units (ARUs) can provide cost-effective, long-term and systematic species monitoring data
for sound-producing wildlife, including birds, amphibians, insects and mammals over large areas. Modern deep
learning can efficiently automate the detection of species occurrences in these sound data with high accuracy.
Further, citizen science can be leveraged to scale up the deployment of ARUs and collect reference vocalizations
needed for training and validating deep learning models. In this study we develop a convolutional neural
network (CNN) acoustic classification pipeline for detecting 54 bird species in Sonoma County, California USA,
with sound and reference vocalization data collected by citizen scientists within the Soundscapes to Landscapes
project ( www.soundscapes2landscapes.org ). We trained three ImageNet-based CNN architectures (MobileNetv2,
ResNet50v2, ResNet100v2), which function as a Mixture of Experts (MoE), to evaluate the usefulness of several
methods to enhance model accuracy. Specifically, we: 1) quantify accuracy with fully-labeled 1-min soundscapes
for an assessment of real-world conditions; 2) assess the effect on precision and recall of additional pre-training
with an external sound archive (xeno-canto) prior to fine-tuning with vocalization data from our study domain;
and, 3) assess how detections and errors are influenced by the presence of coincident biotic and non-biotic
sounds (i.e., soundscape components). In evaluating accuracy with soundscape data ( n = 37 species) across
CNN probability thresholds and models, we found acoustic pre-training followed by fine-tuning improved
average precision by 10.3% relative to no pre-training, although there was a small average 0.8% reduction in
recall. In selecting an optimal CNN architecture for each species based on maximum F( β = 0.5), we found our
MoE approach had total precision of 84.5% and average species precision of 85.1%. Our data exhibit multiple
issues arising from applying citizen science and acoustic monitoring at the county scale, including deployment of
ARUs with relatively low fidelity and recordings with background noise and overlapping vocalizations. In
particular, human noise was significantly associated with more incorrect species detections (false positives,
decreased precision), while physical interference (e.g., recorder hit by a branch) and geophony (e.g., wind) was
associated with the classifier missing detections (false negatives, decreased recall). Our process surmounted these
obstacles, and our final predictions allowed us to demonstrate how deep learning applied to acoustic data from
low-cost ARUs paired with citizen science can provide valuable bird diversity data for monitoring and conser -
vation efforts.
1. Introduction
Biodiversity is under profound stress from climate change, habitat
loss, pollution, and other interconnected factors that now threaten
approximately 25% of species with extinction and others with steep
declines in abundance ( Díaz et al., 2019 ; Dirzo et al., 2014 ; Lecl `ere et al.,
2020 ). For example, in North America, bird abundance is estimated to
have decreased 29% since 1970 ( Rosenberg et al., 2019 ) and worldwide
* Corresponding author.
E-mail address: matthew.clark@sonoma.edu (M.L. Clark).
Contents lists available at ScienceDirect

journal homepage: www.else vier.com/loc ate/ecolinf

Received 11 May 2022; Received in revised form 8 March 2023; Accepted 8 March 2023

[Halaman 2]
Ecological Informatics 75 (2023) 102065
2
there is an estimated decline in populations for 48% of extant bird
species ( Lees et al., 2022 ). To understand these changes and develop
effective solutions, the science and land management communities
require baseline conditions and biodiversity monitoring to track species
distributions, abundances and aggregated indicators of trends at multi -
ple spatial and temporal scales ( Pereira et al., 2013 ). Unfortunately,
adequate biodiversity data are limited, and when present, lack sustained
or repeated sampling. Birds are the most widely monitored animal
species ( Lees et al., 2022 ), with a large amount of data acquired annually
by a robust citizen science community, such as through the global eBird
project ( Sullivan et al., 2014 ) and the U.S. Breeding Bird Survey ( Sauer
et al., 2017 ). However, avian data collected in the field (e.g., point
counts) requires an observer to accurately identify a species by sight or
vocalization, with variability introduced by differences in skill level,
perception of sounds, and ability to see birds ( Catlin-Groves, 2012 ;
Tulloch and Szabo, 2012 ). Further, data collected by volunteers tends to
be spatially clustered ( Mair and Ruete, 2016 ; Tulloch et al., 2013 ), has
high variation in effort and observer skill ( Tulloch and Szabo, 2012 ;
Oliveira et al., 2016 ), and has limited temporal sampling (e.g., on
weekends), thereby limiting scientific applications ( Zhang, 2020 ).
Sound autonomous recording units (ARUs) placed in the field for
days to months can provide long-term and systematic data on the
occurrence and abundance of sound-producing wildlife, including birds,
amphibians, insects and mammals ( Balantic and Donovan, 2020 ; Gibb
et al., 2019 ). Further, ARUs can provide similar estimates of bird rich -
ness as traditional point counts ( Darras et al., 2018 ) and sound re -
cordings are a permanent record that can be re-interpreted as necessary
( Aide et al., 2013 ; Gibb et al., 2019 ). Recorders can be placed on public
lands by volunteers, but also delivered to private landowners for
deployment, thereby increasing sampling across a study region ( Snyder
et al., 2022 ). Leaving ARUs operative for days can generate an immense
amount of data, which becomes a challenge to manual identification of
species by their unique vocalizations, necessitating automated
machine-based detection techniques ( Brandes, 2008 ). Although human
identification of species in sounds has the advantage of much higher
flexibility in the interpretation of sounds, machine-based detection
could potentially overcome the challenges of bias due to variance in
observer skills. For example, in a study of bat sounds, Jennings et al.
(2008) found machine-based identifications overperformed humans in
accuracy of detections. Further, despite the differences in detection
probability between traditional bird point counts and ARU surveys,
presumably due to birds altering their behavior in the presence of
humans, Furnas and Callas (2015) found no differences in species oc -
cupancy estimates for a limited number of species. Thus, the advantages
of using ARUs are mainly the permanent record of the sample, reduced
bias (spatial, temporal, observer skill), and cost-effectiveness.
Automating species detections in sound recordings is a growing field,
and encompasses a range of taxonomic groups, including birds ( Acevedo
et al., 2009 ; Campos-Cerqueira et al., 2017 ; Furnas and Callas, 2015 ),
bats ( Walters et al., 2012 ), amphibians ( Acevedo et al., 2009 ; Campos-
Cerqueira and Aide, 2017 ), and insects ( Aide et al., 2017 ). Priyadarshani
et al. (2018) reviewed first generation techniques, which include steps to
reduce noise, segment bird vocalizations from background, and extract
pre-determined features for training machine learning classifiers. These
features tend to be manually identified by domain experts, limiting
performance compared to more recent approaches that learn the fea -
tures ( Gupta et al., 2021 ). Further, much of this early research used
relatively small datasets with low levels of noise and involved manual
tuning of parameters. As a consequence, the techniques generally have
poor recall rates (i.e., ability to detect all bird sounds), high sensitivity to
noise, and do not generalize with new species, noise conditions or
recording equipment ( Priyadarshani et al., 2018 ; Stowell et al., 2019 ).
Modern deep learning classification based on convolutional neural
networks (CNNs) is relatively new to the field of bioacoustics species
detection (see review by Stowell, 2022 ), and tends to have very high
( > 90%) accuracy for bird species ( Incze et al., 2018 ; Kahl et al., 2021 ;
LeBien et al., 2020 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ; Stowell et al., 2019 ; Zhong et al.,
2020 ). Tuning of the network hyperparameters and convolutional filters
provides automated feature learning, thereby removing an obstacle of
earlier machine learning methods ( Gupta et al., 2021 ). Sound data
include frequency, amplitude and temporal information, and there are
different approaches to express these data in CNN architectures. One
approach is to represent sound data as amplitude-time waveforms, then
train 1-dimensional neural network architectures, such as Recurrent
Neural Networks (RNNs) to identify distinct patterns ( Sang et al., 2018 ;
Weninger and Schuller, 2011 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Another approach is
to train CNNs to classify 2D image spectrograms ( Kahl et al., 2021 ;
LeBien et al., 2020 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ; Stowell et al., 2019 ; Zhong et al.,
2020 ). A popular extension is to use mel-spectrograms from human
speech and music domains, which in the process of computing the
spectrogram, recorded sound frequencies (Hertz) are remapped to a
frequency scale (mel scale) whose intervals are perceptually equidistant
to human hearing ( Gupta et al., 2021 ; Kahl et al., 2021 ; Lasseck, 2019 ;
LeBien et al., 2020 ; Zhong et al., 2020 ). The use of 2D CNN models has
dominated the annual LifeCLEF Bird Recognition Challenge (BirdCLEF)
competition, with an important finding being that architectures adapted
from the image recognition domain do not necessarily need to be deep in
order to effectively classify calls and songs for all bird species ( Kahl
et al., 2021 ), which could simplify model training and implementation.
In our review of peer-reviewed research, we found that a common
deficiency with acoustic bird classification research is the reporting of
overly-optimistic accuracy or a focus on the accuracy metrics that may
not be ideal for biodiversity applications. A common approach is to use a
hold-out set randomly sampled from the same dataset used to train the
models, as a single set (e.g., Zhong et al., 2020 ) or in a k-fold sampling
scheme (e.g., Gupta et al., 2021 ). These test clips are often clean ex -
amples of bird calls and exclude those with non-target sounds, over -
lapping sounds, and background recorder noise, and thus do not depict
actual accuracy when a classifier is deployed on whole recordings in a
real-world application. There has been some progress on reporting more
realistic accuracy in applied settings. LeBien et al. (2020) assigned class
presence within a larger temporal window (i.e., 1 min) based on
thresholds on class probability from finer temporal predictions, i.e., 2 s
with 1-s overlap. However, this method reports accuracy with a different
resolution than the classifier and forces a constraining temporal aggre -
gation. In a CNN-based study focused on bird and other small mammal
vocalizations, Ruff et al. (2021) created a large independent dataset of
spectrogram segments through manual validation, half of which were
non-target sounds and background noise, and 6% included multiple
target species. The applied CNN had 12-s predictions but did not match
the variable temporal sampling of the test data. Since 2019, the Bird -
CLEF competitions have evaluated accuracy with independent “ sound -
scape ” test data, which are continuous recordings with detailed species
annotations from expert ornithologists ( Kahl et al., 2020 ). These test
data are thus a domain shift, and provide an assessment of accuracy
when the classifier is applied to recordings from new environments from
which it was trained ( Kahl et al., 2021 ). Further, it is important for ac -
curacy statistics to be relevant to a particular biodiversity application
( Knight et al., 2020a ). For many biodiversity applications, such as oc -
cupancy modeling or species distribution models, there is a general
requirement to correctly identify the presence of a species from acoustic
data ( Campos-Cerqueira and Aide, 2016 ), but not necessarily all in -
stances of a species vocalizing in a recording. High detection accuracy
reported in some studies come at the cost of high numbers of false
positives that can lead to very inaccurate estimates of occupancy and
biodiversity ( Royle and Link, 2006 ).
Many 2D CNNs use well-labeled training and validation data from
the study domain intended to optimize weights in existing image-based
architectures (e.g., ResNet, VGGish, MobileNet), i.e., transfer learning.
These data are usually hard to acquire and thus have low sample sizes.
This often leads to the use of larger labeled data from outside the study
domain. Recent BirdCLEF competitions use weakly-labeled audio
M.L. Clark et al.

[Halaman 3]
Ecological Informatics 75 (2023) 102065
3
recordings from the open-access xeno-canto (XC) archive ( www.xeno-
canto.org ) for bird species as well as other public audio archives for
background sound, including other animals ( Kahl et al., 2020 ). These
data span a wide range of environmental conditions and recorder types,
allowing the training of a generalized bird species classifier ( Henkel
et al., 2021 ; Kahl et al., 2020 ; Kahl et al., 2022 ; Lasseck, 2019 ). Although
BirdCLEF accuracy is now tested with independent soundscapes, the
accuracy of predictions can increase by over 25% when some training
data come from the soundscapes themselves ( Lasseck, 2019 ). Large
datasets can also be used in an initial pre-training step applied to initial
pre-trained CNN backbones, which can help learn low-level spectrogram
features, followed by fine-tuning with data from target classes from
within the study domain ( Yosinski et al., 2014 ; Quinn et al., 2022 ).
Here we report on a 2D CNN acoustic classification pipeline for
detecting bird species in Sonoma County, California, USA. The sound
and reference data were collected with the help of citizen scientists
within the Soundscapes to Landscapes project ( www.soundscapes2landsc
apes.org ). This aspect of our research introduces several challenges not
found in other studies, such as the use of low-cost recorders, placement
of recorders in various public and private landscapes along an urban-
wildland gradient, and reference vocalizations collected with varying
levels of expertise. An advantage of our study is a collaboration with
expert citizen scientists to label every bird vocalization in a sample of 1-
min recordings (i.e., soundscape data), providing independent test data
for assessing real-world accuracy of our classifiers in our study domain.
We used weakly labeled data from outside our study domain to pre-train
three image-based CNN classifiers to recognize spectrogram-based fea -
tures, followed by fine-tuning with data from our study domain. In
contrast, other studies do not include an intermediary pre-training step
prior to fine tuning. Further, we take advantage of a companion study by
Quinn et al. (2022) that used a deep learning classifier to detect general
soundscape composition components in our audio data. We use these
data to investigate potential sources of coincident sounds that may cause
errors in our bird species classifier. To our knowledge, the pairing of bird
species and soundscape deep-learning classifiers in a unified analytical
framework is a unique contribution of our study.
We trained three ImageNet CNN architectures (MobileNetv2,
ResNet50v2, ResNet100v2), which function as a Mixture of Experts
(MoE), for classifying bird species in our study area. The primary ob -
jectives of our study are to: 1) assess classifier accuracy with fully-
labeled soundscape recordings, and compare this accuracy to an esti -
mate from a reserved set of reference data that were also used to train
CNNs, a common practice in this domain; 2) evaluate the potential
improvement in accuracy by pre-training CNN models using bird vo -
calizations from weakly-labeled XC audio recordings; and, 3) assess how
detections and errors are influenced by the presence of coincident biotic
and non-biotic sounds (i.e., soundscape components). To have a frame of
reference on the relative precision and improvements on our models, we
also compare the performance of our approach against an external
standard. For this we used BirdNET, a global acoustic bird 2D CNN that
is also being developed for citizen science sound data ( Kahl et al., 2021 ).
It is not our intent to evaluate BirdNET performance, as it was not
trained with our data.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Field data collection
In situ acoustics data were acquired in Sonoma County, in northern
California, USA. Sonoma County is 4118 km
2
with a wide variety of land
use/cover types, including agricultural, urban - residential, forest,
chaparral and grassland habitat types ( Fig. 1 ). Recordings were collected
by citizen scientists from 2017 to 2021 during the breeding bird season
(mid-March thru mid-July) when birds tend to vocalize frequently. To
collect acoustic field data, we used two types of ARUs: Android-based LG
smartphones with attached microphones and waterproof cases and
AudioMoths ( Hill et al., 2019 ) enclosed in nylon pouches. ARUs were
deployed at sites for 3 to 5 days, and programmed to record 1 min of
every 10, thus providing temporal sampling through day and night, with
an average of 582 min of recordings per site. There was a total of
735,984 min of recordings from 1236 sites ( Fig. 1 ), with 81% from
AudioMoth and 19% from LG ARUs. Additional details on field data
collection can be found in Snyder et al. (2022) .
2.2. Reference bird vocalizations
2.2.1. Regions of interest (ROI) for classifier fine-tuning training and testing
We targeted 54 species that have distinctly unique vocalizations (call
or song pattern) and are common in the study area during the breeding
bird season ( Table 1 ). Although additional species could have been
studied (~180 species total; Sonoma County Breeding Bird Atlas, 2020 ),
our project did not attempt to be exhaustive given the constraints of a
citizen science project based on volunteer labor. Some species include 2
to 3 different vocalizations (Table S1). Reference bird vocalizations were
collected by citizen scientists using a web-based interface in the Arbi -
mon platform ( Aide et al., 2013 ). In this process, an expert citizen sci -
entist with knowledge of local bird vocalizations identified parts of
spectrograms that represent a target bird vocalization. The system then
used this template region of interest (ROI) and a pattern matching al -
gorithm ( LeBien et al., 2020 ) to find similar ROIs in our archive of sound
recordings. Citizen scientists then validated whether the matched ROIs
contained the target vocalization by visual observation of the spectro -
gram and/or listening to the sound clip. We used a consensus-based vote
for validations from users without bird knowledge, taking the majority
of present or absent votes for up to 5 votes. Expert votes were taken as
truth (i.e., no consensus). More details on this process and final ROIs are
available in Supplemental Section 1 and in Snyder et al. (2022) .
Importantly, by using pattern-matching we might have introduced a
sampling bias because it finds ROIs that are relatively clean due to the
use of a correlation threshold. Despite data augmentation methods, this
bias could lead to potentially lower precision in our models when tested
against a random set of recordings.

2.2.2. Soundscapes for testing the classification in field conditions
To generate independent data to test the accuracy of the CNN model
predictions in field conditions within our study area, citizen scientist
experts created “soundscape data”, which was an exhaustive review of a
stratified random sample of 661 recordings (of 1-min) with every bird
vocalization labeled by the second when it started. More information
about the sampling scheme used to select recordings is provided in
Supplemental Section 2. We compiled 18,992 detections of our 54 spe -
cies in the soundscape data (Table 1). Of these, 37 species had at least 40
vocalization events in the soundscape data for the same call/song types
used in training, and thus we limited our soundscape analyses to these
species, with data from 628 recordings. Because we collected ROI and
soundscape data simultaneously, there were 206 recordings in common
for ROI training and soundscape data. This overlap was limited to 473
out of 32,704 ROIs (1.5%) for the 37 target species in our soundscape
analysis, or 473/44,261 (1.1%) of all ROI training data, available prior
to data augmentation. We acknowledge this artifact could lead to higher
estimates of model precision but note that 1) soundscapes were labeled
independently from ROI labels, 2) data augmentation diluted bias from
these 473 training ROIs, and 3) we found that there was a large differ -
ence in soundscape and ROI accuracy, thus revealing that the effect of
the overlap was minimal. Further, since these soundscape data are from
the same audio domain as the ROI data, accuracy statistics with these
data do not indicate the transferability of our CNN processing pipeline
outside our study domain (e.g., a different location, time period, or
recording device), which differs from the “domain-shift” soundscape
data used in Kahl et al. (2021) and BirdCLEF competitions (Kahl et al.,
2020).

2.3. Mel spectrogram 2D representations of sound data
All training and inference in this study was performed using 2-s
segments of our 1-min recordings. This segment length was deter -
mined by the relatively small widths of our pattern-matching templates
(mean width 1.3 ± 1.0 s across species), initial empirical experimenta -
tion, and a consideration of methods by LeBien et al. (2020) , which used
the same pattern-matching routine for reference data collection.
Our field recordings were acquired at sample rates of either 48 kHz
(AudioMoth) or 44.1 kHz (LG smartphone). Vocalizations of our 54
species did not contain frequency components above ~11 kHz and so we
resampled all our audio data to 22.05 kHz (twice the sampling rate
needed to represent our vocalizations). Mel spectrograms were
computed for 2-s audio clips using the Python librosa package (see
supplemental code for parameters). We used the square of the mel
spectrogram energy values in dB (i.e., the power of the signal) as this
results in visually more distinctive bird calls. Since our CNNs operated
on color images, having been pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset, we
converted the 2-s mel spectrograms to 3-channel (RGB) images using
librosa ’ s default magma colormap, which is perceptually uniform
( Fig. 2 ; Fig. S1).
2.4. CNN pre-training data from xeno-canto recordings
For pre-training of our CNN classification models, described in Sec -
tion 2.6 , we used recordings of bird vocalizations in the XC archive.
These recordings were gathered with various devices and quality, but
required 100% positive identification of bird species. We used a curated
dataset of XC recordings from the 2020 Cornell Birdcall Identification
competition ( Howard et al., 2020 ), from which we selected recordings
for 40 species that were targeted in our study and found in the archive.
These XC recordings were a domain shift from our recordings, as we
focused solely on Sonoma County and used only two types of recording
devices. Unlike our ROI data, the XC recordings were long segments and
not focused on a specific part of a bird ’ s vocalization and thus we sought
an automatic means of isolating discrete sounds within variable-length
recordings. This was accomplished with the auto_detec function in the
R warbleR package ( Araya-Salas and Smith-Vidaurre, 2017 ), which
finds the start and end of vocalizations based on amplitude, duration,
and frequency range parameters. We analyzed signals with an amplitude
threshold of 5%, duration of signal detection (i.e., vocalization duration)
from 0.1 to 2 s, and frequency bandpass of 2 to 9 kHz. The auto_detec
function yielded 444,846 isolated signals, or start/stop times of
vocalizations.
For generating mel-spectrograms from XC vocalizations, we padded
each side of vocalization to be at least 2 s in length, clipped the recording
from the original .wav file, and then appended these clips into one
recording per species. Mel spectrograms were generated at a 2-s interval
from this combined recording following the parameters described in
Section 2.3 . We randomly sampled XC data by species to create a
training and validation set. If there were > 750 vocalizations for a spe -
cies, 150 vocalizations were randomly sampled for a validation set; if
there were fewer than 750 vocalizations, we used 20% of the total for
validation. The remaining XC data were used for training, with an
average of 1608 (minimum = 33; maximum = 5540) per species. We did
not need independent XC test data as accuracy improvements with pre-
training were evaluated with ROI test and soundscape data ( Section
2.8 ).

2.5. CNN fine-tuning data from ROIs
We randomly sampled 50 ROIs per species with “ presence ” to form a
held-out test set for accuracy assessment ( Section 2.8.1 ). The remaining
ROIs with species presence were used to fine-tune the CNN models. We
randomly sampled 100 of these ROIs per species to form a validation set
and the remaining formed a training set, which had on average 887 per
species (min = 349, max = 3094). ROIs that were > 2 s in duration were
used in their entirety. For those that were < 2 s in duration, we expanded
the start/stop (i.e., padded) equally on each side of the ROI to total 2 s.
Different vocalizations for a given species were combined into a single
class per species. If any ROIs were overlapping in time from different
pattern-matching runs for a given species, we placed those ROIs in the
training set to avoid temporal autocorrelation in our validation and test
data.
The recordings for each ROI were cut using start/stop times and
sequentially appended to create a single merged .wav file for each spe -
cies and set (i.e., train, validation) combination. Each merged .wav file
was then sliced into 2-s increments and mel-spectrograms computed.
Note that since there were some ROIs from the pattern matching that
were > 2 s, some 2-s recording clips included parts from different ROIs.
Performing data augmentation on training datasets is a widely used
technique in deep learning, including sound classification applications,
to regularize models and provide more robust features ( Salamon and
Bello, 2017 ). We performed data augmentation by splitting the merged .
wav training file for each species in half and then adding these two
halves sample-wise. This augmented .wav file was similarly split into 2-s
increments as above and mel-spectrograms were computed. The training
dataset increased by 50% after this data augmentation, which is
important for small training datasets such as ours.
At the end of this process, we had training and validation, 2-s mel-
spectrograms that were used to fine-tune the CNN models.
2.6. CNN multi-species classification models
We trained three 2D, image-based CNN models to classify bird spe -
cies based on their vocalizations represented in mel-spectrograms. These
were multi-species models, although we ultimately chose the best model
for each species using soundscape data ( Section 2.8.3 ). The underlying
network backbones were pre-trained on the large ImageNet archive of
labeled images (1.4 M images across 1000 classes) and included Mobi -
leNetv2 ( Sandler et al., 2018 ) with 4.44 M parameters, ResNet50v2 ( He
et al., 2016 ) with 23.65 M parameters, and ResNet101v2 with 42.71 M
parameters. We chose these architectures as they were widely used in
the literature ( Stowell, 2022 ) and provided a contrast between smaller
(more generalist) and larger (more specialist) architectures. When there
is a large amount of training data for transfer learning, the larger ResNet
networks perform better than the smaller MobileNet networks due to
their capacity ( Khan et al., 2020 ). However, in our case, the ROI refer -
ence data available for training were limited, so we sought to explore
different network sizes in conjunction with pre-training with additional
acoustic reference data from outside of our audio domain, followed by
fine-tuning with ROI data from our study site.
We evaluated model performance with and without additional pre-
training with external sound data prior to fine-tuning with sound data
from our study. For the pre-trained models, we used training and vali -
dation XC mel-spectrograms to adjust the weights of each of the three
CNN models. Pre-training with XC data was implemented for all CNN
models starting with training the final, dense layer for 10 epochs fol -
lowed by training all layers for 10 additional epochs.
Fine-tuning using the ROI training and validation mel-spectrograms
was then applied to both the default CNN backbones (i.e., not pre-
trained on XC) and to the XC pre-trained CNNs. The fine-tuning pro -
cess consisted of two stages: (1) model training on the classifier only (i.
e., dense, fully-connected layer), freezing all other trainable parameters
in CNN layers for 10 epochs (learning rate = 0.0001), and (2) fine-tuning
the network by unfreezing all layers and training for 10 more epochs.
Model weights were saved only when the internal validation loss
decreased.
All fully-trained CNNs produced a vector of 54 predicted probabili -
ties using a binary cross entropy classifier with sigmoid activation (one
value for each species). We applied thresholds to these probabilities to
evaluate model accuracy ( Section 2.8 ).
2.7. Inference on whole recording archive
We applied the fine-tuned CNNs at a 2-s window with 1-s overlap,
yielding 59 mel-spectrograms for each 1-min recording. This resulted in
> 43 million mel-spectrograms from all recordings. Inference on each
mel-spectrogram generated 54 probability values (one for each species),
for each of the three models, with fine-tuning with ROI data on both
default ImageNet and XC pre-trained versions. Given this large data
volume to process and analyze, we performed CNN inference on a high-
performance cluster and stored our results in a MySQL database for
rapid retrieval. We further pre-filtered all predictions into an informa -
tive set by archiving only those with a sigmoid probability ≥ 0.65.
2.8. Evaluation of accuracy
2.8.1. Evaluation of accuracy with ROI test data
The ROI test data consisted of 50 presences and 50 absences for each
species. In the accuracy assessment, we used the ROI length as deter -
mined by pattern matching template for a given bird species. Presences
were the group of randomly-sampled ROIs set aside for testing that were
never used to train the models. We assumed that if the species was
evaluated by citizen scientists as absent in the ROI, then the target bird
was not there. Two possible sources of error might have been introduced
when determining absences for a target species. First, our citizen sci -
entists could have failed to detect the target species in the ROI due to
noise or otherwise unclear patterns. Absences were based on consensus
votes or expert review, and we are confident that this source of error is
minimal. Second, our citizen scientists assessed matches for a species
within the range of frequencies found in its pattern matching template,
which was focused on common vocalizations in our region. Birds, among
other animals, are known to shift frequencies in order to adapt to a noisy
or competitive soundscape ( Bermúdez-Cuamatzin et al., 2011 ; Roca
et al., 2016 ). It is possible that the target birds were not detected by
pattern matching if their vocalizations were outside the range of the
template, and therefore never assessed by the citizen scientists. How -
ever, the range of frequency shifts reported in the literature are rela -
tively small (200 – 500 Hz, e.g. Luther et al., 2016 ) compared to the
frequency ranges in our templates (~1.5 to 7 KHz, depending on the
species). Any frequency shift would likely be included in the template
frequency range and inspected by citizen scientists as a presence or
absence. Further, because of the county scale of our sound collection, we
do not expect that variations in vocalization (e.g., dialects) for a given
bird species would fall outside of the search frequency-band for a given
species. Thus, we are confident that a detection of a target bird for an
absence is indeed a FP.
We randomly selected absences from the same set of recordings in
which we found presences across all species. A given recording may or
may not have included absences and presences for the same species, and
may contain labels from one or more species. In the accuracy assess -
ment, the species prediction for an ROI was retrieved from a CNN model
for species detected with probabilities ≥ 0.65 (i.e., 65%). That is, for
each ROI of a species, we took the highest value of the predictions for
that species at the center second and one second before and after the
center of the ROI. We also retrieved the predicted probabilities for all
other species in the same time interval. The 0.65 minimum threshold
was intended as a filter for informative rather than random (i.e., ≤ 0.50)
predictions. We calculated true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false
negatives (FN), precision (TP/[TP + FP]), and recall (TP/[TP + FN]) for
M.L. Clark et al.

[Halaman 7]
Ecological Informatics 75 (2023) 102065
7
a range of CNN probability thresholds (i.e., 0.65 to 0.99). For ROI
presences, if a species was detected with a CNN probability higher than a
given threshold that matched the target ROI species label, the sample
was a TP; otherwise, the sample was considered a FN for that species. For
ROI absences, if a species was detected that matched the target ROI
label, the sample was considered a FP for that species. We did not expect
the ROI data to adequately represent species vocalizations that overlap
those from other bird species, or soundscape components more broadly.
Instead, our ROI test data included only relatively clean (as perceived by
a human observer) presences and absences. It follows that the perfor -
mance results against the ROI data would be higher than the more
realistic soundscape data, which were from an exhaustive review of
recordings for target vocalizations and include samples with a range of
soundscape conditions ( Section 2.8.2 ).
2.8.2. Evaluation of accuracy with soundscape data and BirdNET
A benefit of our soundscape data was that they included labels of all
bird vocalizations (i.e., calls and songs) within a 1-min recording,
including those with temporal overlap. We matched manually-detected
soundscape vocalizations to 2-s predictions found within a 1-s and 3-s
window before and after the vocalization ’ s start time, respectively.
The species label of the soundscape vocalization and all probability
values within the temporal window were used to determine the accuracy
of the model predictions over a range of probability threshold values, as
we did with the ROI test data. These predictions were used to evaluate
total precision and average species (class) precision. Although sound -
scape data used in our accuracy assessment included vocalizations that
overlap in the same time period of the recording, we did not assess this
factor in our analyses.
In comparing ROI and soundscape accuracy, we acknowledge that
some difference could be related to variable sample size among species
between the two datasets. However, we believe this effect is minimal as
we used well-randomized representative samples of soundscapes and
report total precision and recall across species. Since these measures are
aggregated raw counts of TP, FP, and FN, if our soundscape data and ROI
test datasets were properly randomized and if they result in represen -
tative performances for each class, it follows that the difference in per -
formances shown in the evaluation metric curves is expected to be
insensitive to class imbalances in the soundscape data. Further, we
report average class precision and recall statistics at optimal thresholds
( Section 2.8.3 ), which are less influenced by differences in positives in
each dataset.
We also compared the soundscape accuracy of our XC pre-trained,
fine-tuned CNN models (hereafter CNN-XC) against the leading Bird -
NET CNN classifier ( Kahl et al., 2021 ). This is a ResNet, spectrogram-
based multi-species classifier of 984 birds from North America and
Europe. We used the BirdNet Analyzer version 2.2 ( https://github.
com/kahst/BirdNET-Analyzer ) to predict bird species in our sound -
scape data. The BirdNET processing pipeline is designed to make pre -
dictions in 3-s clips, which we processed with 2-s overlap, resulting in 57
samples for each soundscape recording. We ran the process with default
settings with and without geographic location set for the center of
Sonoma County (38.5780
◦
N, 122.9888
◦
W), and considered all species
predicted over a given sigmoid probability threshold within each sample
as present. We used start times of soundscape vocalizations for matching
BirdNET species predictions. To better match our process of evaluating
soundscape accuracy with our CNN models, we split each BirdNET 3-s
prediction into two 2-s predictions with 1-s overlap. Precision and
recall curves were generated by varying the BirdNET probabilities as we
did with our CNN models, for both predictions with and without the
geographic filter. In contrast to the evaluation of our CNN models, when
testing BirdNET predictions we included all vocalization types for our
target bird species (i.e., we did not filter them to those used in training
our CNN models).
2.8.3. Optimal model and threshold selection
Our next step was to evaluate the effect of soundscape components
on the precision and recall of our CNN-XC models ( Section 2.9 ). To do
this, we sought an optimal model and threshold for each species sepa -
rately. Most studies seek models that balance precision, or how many
positive predictions are correct, and recall, or how many of the true
predictions are retrieved (also referred to as sensitivity or true positive
rate). In this context, accuracy is often reported as a F β score, or (1 + β
2
)
× (precision × recall)/( β
2
× precision + recall), which gives equal
weight to both measures when β = 1, i.e., the F1 score. Precision is a
more important metric for most applied biodiversity applications as it
decreases with more FP, i.e., the species being predicted as present when
it is not there. A more practical target for biodiversity monitoring could
be stated as, for example, a classifier with > 80% precision and > 20%
recall, or an alternative form of F β score, such as β = 0.5 (F0.5), which
places more weight on precision over recall ( Kahl et al., 2021 ). Here we
report optimal probability thresholds by selecting those that maximize
F0.5 scores using soundscape data. Precision and recall were computed
for each CNN model on a species (class) level, as well as for all species
combined (total precision and recall).
For the 37 species in our soundscape analysis ( Section 2.2.2 ), we
picked the model and associated threshold that produced the highest
F0.5 score. For the remaining 17 species, we averaged maximum-F0.5
probability thresholds from MobileNet, since this architecture was
selected as optimal for the majority of species. Future research could
sample more soundscapes to retrieve sufficient detections needed to
refine optimal model selection and thresholds for these 17 species. We
applied these optimal models and thresholds to soundscape ( n = 37
species) and ROI data ( n = 54 species) and reported class precision and
recall.
2.9. Analysis of bird detections with coincident soundscape components
We sought to provide additional insight on how bird detections from
optimal CNN models were influenced by other types of sounds. For this
analysis, we associated bird species detections and non-detections from
our soundscape data with the presence of soundscape components:
human noise from automobiles, airplanes, etc. (Anthropophony); wild -
life vocalizations, including birds, amphibians and insects (Biophony);
weather phenomena, such as wind and rain (Geophony), quiet periods
with mainly background recorder noise or faint sounds (Quiet); and,
abrupt noise from physical contact, such as from branches banging the
recorder from wind (Interference). These soundscape components are
collectively called ABGQI. Our companion study by Quinn et al. (2022)
describes using an independent CNN and associated thresholds devel -
oped for the same sound data in our study domain. Briefly, the ABGQI
classier was pre-trained on XC data and fine-tuned with sound reference
data from our audio data (same domain). The classifier achieved an
overall F0.75-score of 0.88, precision of 0.94, and recall of 0.80 across
the ABGQI classes.
The ABGQI classifier was then applied to the same 2-s clips used for
bird detections. We used the search window for matching bird de -
tections to our soundscape data ( Section 2.8.2 ) and marked if a given
sample had any ABGQI classes detected in the search window. Sound -
scape components were associated with labels of TP, FP, or FN for bird
species within samples, allowing us to look at how bird detections and
errors are associated with coincident biotic and non-biotic sounds. We
tested the influence of ABGQI and species on TP, FP and FN, respec -
tively, using separate logistic generalized linear mixed models for each
case (see Supplemental Section 3). The “ TP model ” set as response value
1 for TP and FN or FP were assigned 0. This inference sought to un -
derstand the effect of soundscape components in obtaining a correct
classification vs not. The “ FN model ” treated FN as 1 and TP as 0, and did
not include FP data, so that inference was limited to understanding the
effect of ABGQI on a resulting FN instead of a correct detection. Simi -
larly, the “ FP model ” treated FP as 1 and TP as 0 to evaluate the effect of
M.L. Clark et al.

[Halaman 8]
Ecological Informatics 75 (2023) 102065
8
sound components on error of commission vs a correct detection and did
not include the FN data. In all models, species and 1-min recording name
were treated as random effects. Note that recording name encompasses
the variation among sites, temporal differences, and recorder type (LG
vs. AudioMoth), so it accounts for more than just possible error corre -
lations from the same recording. The random species effect accounts for
any species-level effects on the results.
3. Results
3.1. Effect of pre-training CNN models with xeno-canto data prior to fine-
tuning
When assessed with test ROIs, the pre-training of CNN models with
auxiliary XC mel-spectrograms, followed by fine-tuning (i.e., CNN-XC
models) with training ROIs improved total recall (all species together)
by an average of 5.9% and slightly increased total precision by an
average of 0.2% relative to not including the XC pre-training step,
considering all three models and probability thresholds from 0.65 to
0.99 ( Fig. 3 - ROI). However, when tested against the soundscape data,
there was an average 0.8% decrease in total recall and an average 10.3%
increase in total precision with XC pre-training ( Fig. 3 - Soundscape).
Given that we sought high precision when applied to a real-world
inference scenario (i.e., a soundscape), we focus our results on CNN-
XC models for the remainder of our analysis.
3.2. Differences between ROI and soundscape accuracy with CNN-XC
models
When assessed for all species, we found total precision (all species
combined) as measured using ROI test data was very high across all
probability thresholds ( Fig. 4 - ROI). For example, at a threshold of 0.99,
total precision and average species precision with ROI data was 99.4%
and 97.3% for MobileNet, 99.2% and 99.1% for ResNet50v2, and 99.1%
and 99.1% for ResNet101v2, respectively. In contrast, when tested using
all soundscape data, precision was considerably lower ( Fig. 4 - Sound -
scape). At a 0.99 threshold, total precision and average species precision
with soundscape data was 76.7% and 86.6% for MobileNet, 78.5% and
88.8% for ResNet50v2, and 76.1% and 86.6% for ResNet101v2,
respectively. In the worst case, species PAWR at the 0.99 threshold had
an average precision of 100.0% across models when tested with ROI
data, while average precision was 48.7% with soundscape data. We thus
conclude that the standard approach to estimating accuracy with a hold-
out set of sample data from the same dataset as the training/validation
data (i.e., ROIs) greatly overestimates performance of CNN models.
3.3. Comparison with BirdNET
When tested against soundscape data, all three of our CNN-XC
models had slightly lower total precision than BirdNET with the
geographic filter (max = 81.8% at 0.65 threshold), and CNN-XC models
performed better than BirdNET without the filter (max = 69.6% at 0.74
threshold; Fig. 5 A). However, all CNN-XC models had higher recall than
both BirdNET versions, regardless of thresholds. At a 0.99 threshold,
CNN-XC models had an average 13.9% higher total precision and 27.6%
higher total recall than BirdNET with the geographic filter ( Fig. 5 B). We
found BirdNET total precision had very little sensitivity to thresholds up
to 0.90, while precision declined at higher thresholds as FN increased
more than FP ( Fig. 5 A, BirdNET). The BirdNET classifier with a
geographic filter had sufficient total recall, which we set at 20% for our
application, only at thresholds at or below 0.71, with a corresponding
average total precision of 81.2% below this point. In contrast, our CNN-
XC models had a total recall of over 20% at all thresholds; and, at the
0.99 threshold, average total precision was 77.1% and average total
recall was 28.2% among models ( Fig. 5 B). Since BirdNET was not
trained with data from our domain, these comparisons are not strictly
appropriate, yet they provide assurance that our models perform well
overall relative to this well-developed standard. Our results also high -
light the importance of using BirdNET with a geographic filter for
improved precision.
3.4. Optimal model selection for each species
We used soundscape data to select the optimal model with the cor -
responding threshold that produced the highest F0.5 score. We found
that different optimal models were chosen for each species ( Figs. 6 & 7 ).
For example, MobileNetv2 was selected for CAVI, ResNet101v2 for
WEME, and ResNet50v2 for CAQU ( Fig. 6 ). The MobileNet architecture
was the most common optimal model in our soundscape data (17 of 37
species; Fig. 7 ), with an average F0.5 of 0.80 and average threshold of
0.79 ( Table 2 ).
Based on soundscape data, total precision (pooled across species)
with optimal CNN-XC model selection was 84.5%. Species precision
ranged from 46.9% (SOSP) to 100.0% (COYE, MOUQ, and WIWA), with
average species precision of 85.1 ± 13.2% ( Fig. 8 A). Total recall (pooled
across classes) with optimal models was 60.0% and average species

3.5. Influence of soundscape components on bird species detections and
model error
With optimal thresholds ( Section 3.4 ) applied to soundscapes, we
associated bird detections (TP, FP) and non-detections (FN) with
broader sound categories detected by an independent CNN ( Quinn et al.,
2022 ) within the same samples of soundscape data ( Fig. 9 ). Detailed
logistic regression model results are found in Supplemental Section 3.
Our TP model had highly significant positive effects of Biophony
(coeff. = 0.731, z = 9.53, p < 0.0001) on correctly identifying bird
species, and there was a high prevalence of Biophony associated with TP
( Fig. 9 ). Indeed, the presence of Biophony doubled the odds of a TP
detection. This result is expected as Biophony includes birds, as well as
other animal vocalizations, and should be trigged by the target species
vocalization; however, we are unable to determine from these data if
there were overlapping biotic sounds with target bird vocalizations.
Other sound components had all highly significant negative effects (all p
< 0.0001), principally from Geophony (coeff. = ␀ 0.57, z = ␀ 4.71),
followed by (in order), Quiet (coeff. = ␀ 0.54, z = ␀ 4.84), Interference
(coeff. = ␀ 0.50, z = ␀ 4.79), and Anthropophony (coeff. = ␀ 0.38, z =
␀ 4.03). These effects reduced the odds of a TP by about 40% each
individually, the worst being Geophony with 43%, and least being
Anthrophony with a 31% less chance of a TP detection.
The odds of a FP (vs TP) result were 31.3%. The FP model revealed a
highly significant positive influence of Anthropophony (coeff. = 0.89, z
= 6.08, p < 0.0001), more than doubling the odds (244%) of a FP result

4. Discussion
4.1. Overall performance of bird vocalization models
An ultimate goal of the Soundscapes to Landscapes project is to
monitor bird species richness at sample sites using sound recordings
from low-cost ARUs. As a step toward this goal, we applied image-based
deep learning models (CNNs) for automated detection of 54 bird species
from their vocalizations. We prioritized detecting species with confi -
dence at sites, as opposed to capturing all detections in every second of
our 1-min recordings. We thus evaluated accuracy with a focus on
precision and F0.5 scores, as these measures place more emphasis on
true positives and penalize false positives. We evaluated accuracy with
test samples, i.e., ROI data, that were focused on individual vocaliza -
tions and generated by an automated detection algorithm, and evaluated
with consensus-based voting by both expert and regular citizen scien -
tists. Further, we evaluated accuracy against an independent sample of
1-min recordings from the same sound domain with complete labeling of
bird calls by our expert citizen scientists, i.e., soundscape data. These

data included both non-bird sounds and overlapping vocalizations, thus
providing a realistic test of real-world conditions in our study area and
environmental conditions, but not outside of this domain ( Kahl et al.,
2021 ).
Pre-training with auxiliary XC data resulted in improved evaluation
metrics leading to our conclusion that this step helped improve final
models. The XC archive is global, open access, and driven by bird en -
thusiasts, and in the year 2023 included > 740,000 recordings and >
10,500 species ( xeno-canto.org ). These data include recordings with a
wide variation in quality and recording devices, which can be beneficial
for applied research ( Vellinga and Planqu ´e, 2015 ), and are a significant
source of training data for BirdCLEF competitions and BirdNET ( Kahl
et al., 2020, 2021, 2022 ). Further, we demonstrated an automated
approach to segment sound events in these recordings, thereby making
the data accessible for use in CNN development without a high pre-
processing cost. A rigorous evaluation of why CNN-XC models
increased precision and recall is beyond the scope of our study. How -
ever, we speculate that the XC pre-training step helps the CNN model to
learn mel-spectrogram image features from bird vocalizations. The fine-
tuning step using study-specific mel spectrograms included local prop -
erties within our study region (e.g., bird dialects, non-bird sounds, and
ARU sound fidelity properties), which improved the final layers of the
CNN-XC.
When we selected the best CNN-XC model per species based on the
highest F0.5 score, the overall F0.5 score was 0.78 and the class average
was 0.77 when tested with soundscape data. In comparison, Kahl et al.
(2021) found, using 286 h of fully-annotated audio (i.e., soundscapes),
their BirdNET classifier had an F0.5 score of 0.41 on all 24 h and 0.40 on
a dawn chorus subset, the latter of which included more and overlapping
vocalizations. As with most studies across this research domain, there
are differences in testing methodology and data. First, the BirdNET
classifier is for 984 bird species across North America and Europe,
whereas our study is focused on 54 species in a smaller region. The
BirdNET study used randomly selected 1-h recordings for real-world
soundscape testing, with predictive averages in 5-s segments. Impor -
tantly, these data were from a different domain and included 30 Swift
recorders in a one-square-mile area, whereas BirdNET training was
based on global recordings from a diverse range of recorders and mostly
focused on a single species vocalization. In contrast, our soundscape
data were sampled from recordings from 2017 to 2019, from 6 a.m. to 8
p.m. with oversampling of diverse dawn chorus recordings amounting to
628 1-min recordings with 1-s annotations from 343 unique sites around
Sonoma County. When we assessed BirdNET directly with our
soundscape data, we found the classifier to have much less recall than
our CNN models, although BirdNET precision was higher with relatively
low levels of recall. This result is expected due to the high domain
specificity of CNN models ( Pouyanfar et al., 2018 ). Future research
could assess the potential boost in accuracy by using BirdNET fine-tuned
with domain-specific sound data.
For comparison with other studies, we also assessed accuracy of our
CNN-XC models using independent test data that were a hold-out set
from the same data used for training and validation (i.e., ROI data). Our
ROI total precision (0.99 threshold) was over 99% and class-average
precision was over 97% for all three model architectures. This result is
similar to LeBien et al. (2020) , who used the same Arbimon pattern-
matching routine used in our study and trained a multi-species CNN
classifier (24 bird and frog species) that, when tested with ROIs, had a
total precision of 98% and class-average precision of 90% at a 0.99
probability threshold. In a study of 14 forest birds and mammals, Ruff
et al. (2021) trained a CNN model with precision exceeding 90% at high
probability thresholds when tested against spectrograms with up to four
target classes including birds, mammals, and noise. The use of a hold-out
set for testing is typical in the bioacoustic classification field, yet these
tests are positively biased in that sound clips generally come from high-
quality recordings and include target species with no overlapping
sounds ( Kahl et al., 2021 ). Our use of pattern matching to collect ROIs
focused clip selection on a particular frequency bandwidth and duration,
as determined by the template vocalization. We scanned 66% of our
sound archive with these templates, thereby encompassing high varia -
tion in soundscapes from our study area, including non-bird sounds.
However, since we selected highly correlated matches, clips generally
do not include overlapping bird vocalizations in the frequency band,
faint vocalizations, or excessive noise. In contrast, our soundscape data
included more variation in test cases, including faint calls, ambient
noise, and overlapping vocalizations, generating a more robust accuracy
assessment. To our knowledge, no studies have shown this decline in
accuracy between hold-out test data (ROI) and soundscapes from the
same sound domain. Testing against soundscape data from outside the
domain can further yield more insight into the transferability of classi -
fiers to new conditions, as found in recent BirdCLEF competitions ( Kahl
et al., 2020, 2021, 2022 ).
While many studies in this domain use curated recordings, often
from natural habitats, our sites span a range of land cover and land use
types across an urban-wildland gradient, and thus include high levels of
non-target biophony (e.g., other birds, insects, amphibians, mammals),
anthropophony, geophony, and physical interference noise ( Quinn
